intuition: Put the values in a set so you can quickly check whether a number exists. Begin counting a consecutive run only at a value whose previous number is absent. This avoids counting the same long run again from every point inside it.

The potential trap is repeatedly walking the same run. If values 1 through 1000 exist, starting a forward scan at every value repeats most of that run and becomes quadratic. Begin only at a value whose predecessor is absent; that value is the unique beginning of its maximal run.

From a certified start, increase current until membership fails. The difference current-value is the run length. Every set value belongs to one maximal run and is walked from that run’s unique start, so total walking work is linear even though the algorithm contains a loop inside a loop.

steps: For [100,4,200,1,3,2], the set contains six unique values; their iteration order does not affect the answer.
Value 1 has no predecessor 0, so it starts a run. Membership succeeds for 1, 2, 3, and 4.
Membership fails at 5. The length is current-value=5-1=4, and best becomes 4.
Values 2, 3, and 4 are skipped as starts because each has its predecessor in the set.
Values 100 and 200 each begin a one-value run. Neither improves best, so the final result is 4.

current is the first absent value after the run, so subtracting the starting value gives exactly the count of consecutive present integers.

keyDecision: Start a run at x only when x - 1 is absent. Then count x, x + 1, and so on.

concept.question: Why should a consecutive run begin only where its predecessor is missing?
intuition: Starting a count at every present value repeatedly walks the same long run. Sorting would avoid that repetition but uses more time than membership checks need.

concept.observation: Start a run only when its immediately smaller value is absent.
approach: Build a membership set of the values.
From each value with no predecessor, count upward until the next value is absent.
concept.correctness: Each maximal consecutive run has exactly one value lacking a predecessor. The method starts there and walks every value in that run once. Skipping all other starts prevents repeated run walks but loses no run. Taking the greatest counted length therefore gives the correct result.

complexity.explanation: Membership operations take constant expected time. Every distinct value is walked in one run and tested as a possible start, giving expected linear work and linear set memory.

pitfalls: Consecutive values need not be adjacent in the input.
Duplicates do not add to run length.
